region_scene_page.compact: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish.
region_scene_page.standard: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish. Gene Vincent's Be-Bop-A-Lula, Elvis Presley's Baby Let's Play House, Carl Perkins' Blue Suede Shoes, and Johnny Cash's Folsom Prison Blues give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
region_scene_page.deep: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish. Compared with broader early rock, this lane feels more wiry and local: slapped bass, echo, hiccuped vocals, lean drums, sharp guitar breaks, and very little orchestral cushion. Gene Vincent's Be-Bop-A-Lula, Elvis Presley's Baby Let's Play House, Carl Perkins' Blue Suede Shoes, and Johnny Cash's Folsom Prison Blues give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

mission_detail_history_module.compact: What this route tests: A stripped 1950s guitar-and-slapback lane where country boogie, blues, R&B, and hillbilly flash become urgent rock records.
mission_detail_history_module.standard: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish. Sun Records is the best-known center, but the vocabulary spreads through Carl Perkins, Gene Vincent, Johnny Burnette, Eddie Cochran, Duane Eddy, Link Wray, and other records that make guitar attitude the event. mission_detail_history_module.deep: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish. Sun Records is the best-known center, but the vocabulary spreads through Carl Perkins, Gene Vincent, Johnny Burnette, Eddie Cochran, Duane Eddy, Link Wray, and other records that make guitar attitude the event. scene_description.compact: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish.
scene_description.standard: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish. Gene Vincent's Be-Bop-A-Lula, Elvis Presley's Baby Let's Play House, Carl Perkins' Blue Suede Shoes, and Johnny Cash's Folsom Prison Blues give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
scene_description.deep: Rockabilly came out of small labels, Southern studios, young players, and quick takes that prized feel over polish. Compared with broader early rock, this lane feels more wiry and local: slapped bass, echo, hiccuped vocals, lean drums, sharp guitar breaks, and very little orchestral cushion. Gene Vincent's Be-Bop-A-Lula, Elvis Presley's Baby Let's Play House, Carl Perkins' Blue Suede Shoes, and Johnny Cash's Folsom Prison Blues give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

region_scene_page.compact: Doo-wop grew through Black and Italian American urban vocal groups, neighborhood singing, R&B labels, and pop radio.
region_scene_page.standard: Doo-wop grew through Black and Italian American urban vocal groups, neighborhood singing, R&B labels, and pop radio. The Chords' Sh-Boom, The Penguins' Earth Angel, The Spaniels' Goodnite, Sweetheart, Goodnite, and The Moonglows' Sincerely give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
region_scene_page.deep: Doo-wop grew through Black and Italian American urban vocal groups, neighborhood singing, R&B labels, and pop radio. The arrangement is the signature: the backing voices do not just decorate the lead, they create rhythm, harmony, atmosphere, and emotional commentary. The Chords' Sh-Boom, The Penguins' Earth Angel, The Spaniels' Goodnite, Sweetheart, Goodnite, and The Moonglows' Sincerely give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

mission_detail_history_module.compact: What this route tests: A vocal-group oldies road where harmony, syllables, bass voices, and lead-voice drama carry the whole record.
mission_detail_history_module.standard: Doo-wop grew through Black and Italian American urban vocal groups, neighborhood singing, R&B labels, and pop radio. Some records are rough street-corner performances, while others, like The Platters, polish the language into elegant crossover ballads. It helps place this road in a broader music-history context.
mission_detail_history_module.deep: Doo-wop grew through Black and Italian American urban vocal groups, neighborhood singing, R&B labels, and pop radio. Some records are rough street-corner performances, while others, like The Platters, polish the language into elegant crossover ballads. It made group vocals a rock and pop engine. Later girl groups, soul harmony, Motown, beach harmonies, and oldies radio all inherit its call-and-response design.

atlas_home_region_card.compact: A compact early-1960s pop-craft ecosystem where professional writers, producers, publishers, studio musicians, labels, and young vocal groups turned teen emotion into highly engineered two-and-a-half-minute records.

mission_detail_history_module.standard: The Brill Building label points to a New York songwriting-and-publishing system more than to one literal room or one fixed sound. Around the late 1950s and early 1960s, writers and teams around the Broadway/Times Square publishing world—Goffin/King, Greenwich/Barry, Mann/Weil, Bacharach/David, and others—worked with producers, A&R people, labels, and performers to create records for girl groups, teen idols, pop-soul singers, and dance-craze acts. The girl-group side sharpened the formula: big hooks, direct teenage feeling, cinematic mini-dramas, handclaps, call-and-response, dramatic intros, and production that could make a small song feel huge. It helps place this road in a broader music-history context.

region_scene_page.compact: Early soul-pop crossover sits between first-wave rock and the later soul/funk universe.
region_scene_page.standard: Early soul-pop crossover sits between first-wave rock and the later soul/funk universe. Jackie Wilson's Reet Petite, Sam Cooke's You Send Me, Barrett Strong's Money (That's What I Want), and The Isley Brothers' Shout give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
region_scene_page.deep: Early soul-pop crossover sits between first-wave rock and the later soul/funk universe. Compared with doo-wop or teen-idol pop, the lead voice carries more church-derived urgency, the groove is heavier, and the arrangement often balances raw feeling with pop elegance. Jackie Wilson's Reet Petite, Sam Cooke's You Send Me, Barrett Strong's Money (That's What I Want), and The Isley Brothers' Shout give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

scene_description.compact: Early soul-pop crossover sits between first-wave rock and the later soul/funk universe.
scene_description.standard: Early soul-pop crossover sits between first-wave rock and the later soul/funk universe. Jackie Wilson's Reet Petite, Sam Cooke's You Send Me, Barrett Strong's Money (That's What I Want), and The Isley Brothers' Shout give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
scene_description.deep: Early soul-pop crossover sits between first-wave rock and the later soul/funk universe. Compared with doo-wop or teen-idol pop, the lead voice carries more church-derived urgency, the groove is heavier, and the arrangement often balances raw feeling with pop elegance. Jackie Wilson's Reet Petite, Sam Cooke's You Send Me, Barrett Strong's Money (That's What I Want), and The Isley Brothers' Shout give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

region_scene_page.compact: The Searchers and Hollies show the British guitar-pop side; The Byrds turn the sound into a Los Angeles folk-rock engine.
region_scene_page.standard: The Searchers and Hollies show the British guitar-pop side; The Byrds turn the sound into a Los Angeles folk-rock engine. region_scene_page.deep: The Searchers and Hollies show the British guitar-pop side; The Byrds turn the sound into a Los Angeles folk-rock engine. The archetype sits between beat groups and folk-rock: less raw than garage, less orchestral than baroque pop, and more guitar-texture-driven than harmony pop alone. The Byrds' I'll Feel a Whole Lot Better, We Five's You Were on My Mind, The Cyrkle's Red Rubber Ball, and The Beatles' I Feel Fine give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

The Byrds' I'll Feel a Whole Lot Better, We Five's You Were on My Mind, The Cyrkle's Red Rubber Ball, and The Beatles' I Feel Fine give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. scene_description.deep: After the British Invasion, countless local groups made fast, rough records for regional labels. The lane is song-first and texture-first: fuzz guitar, Farfisa organ, stomp rhythm, nasal vocals, and riffs simple enough to become slogans. The Music Explosion's Little Bit O' Soul, The Seeds' Pushin' Too Hard, ? and the Mysterians' 96 Tears, and The Standells' Dirty Water give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. region_scene_page.compact: Baroque pop does not mean classical music pasted onto rock.
region_scene_page.standard: Baroque pop does not mean classical music pasted onto rock. The Beach Boys' Caroline No, The Beatles' Eleanor Rigby, Love's Alone Again Or, and Bee Gees' Words give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
region_scene_page.deep: Baroque pop does not mean classical music pasted onto rock. The lane is polished but fragile: orchestration, harmony, and bittersweet melody matter more than volume or jam energy. The Beach Boys' Caroline No, The Beatles' Eleanor Rigby, Love's Alone Again Or, and Bee Gees' Words give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

mission_detail_history_module.compact: What this route tests: A 1960s ornate-pop road where chamber instruments, studio craft, close harmony, and emotional precision make pop feel miniature and grand at once.
mission_detail_history_module.standard: Baroque pop does not mean classical music pasted onto rock. It means pop writers and producers using strings, harpsichord colors, unusual chord movement, and careful arrangements to give short songs a chamber-world glow. The Beach Boys, Left Banke, Zombies, Love, Procol Harum, and early Bee Gees each approach that glow differently. It helps place this road in a broader music-history context.
mission_detail_history_module.deep: Baroque pop does not mean classical music pasted onto rock. It means pop writers and producers using strings, harpsichord colors, unusual chord movement, and careful arrangements to give short songs a chamber-world glow. The Beach Boys, Left Banke, Zombies, Love, Procol Harum, and early Bee Gees each approach that glow differently. It made studio arrangement a form of pop authorship and helped prepare the way for progressive rock, chamber pop, sophisticated indie, and artful singer-songwriter studio craft.

scene_description.compact: The Allman Brothers Band, Lynyrd Skynyrd, ZZ Top, Marshall Tucker Band, and related artists made Southern rock broad enough to include improvisational jams, hard anthems, roadhouse boogie, and rootsy storytelling.
scene_description.standard: The Allman Brothers Band, Lynyrd Skynyrd, ZZ Top, Marshall Tucker Band, and related artists made Southern rock broad enough to include improvisational jams, hard anthems, roadhouse boogie, and rootsy storytelling. Lynyrd Skynyrd's Simple Man, The Marshall Tucker Band's Heard It in a Love Song, The Allman Brothers Band's Midnight Rider, and ZZ Top's La Grange give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
scene_description.deep: The Allman Brothers Band, Lynyrd Skynyrd, ZZ Top, Marshall Tucker Band, and related artists made Southern rock broad enough to include improvisational jams, hard anthems, roadhouse boogie, and rootsy storytelling. The guitars often converse rather than simply stack. Lynyrd Skynyrd's Simple Man, The Marshall Tucker Band's Heard It in a Love Song, The Allman Brothers Band's Midnight Rider, and ZZ Top's La Grange give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

scene_description.compact: Country-pop has appeared in waves, from smooth crossover singers to 1990s blockbuster albums and younger artists moving between country and pop markets.
scene_description.standard: Country-pop has appeared in waves, from smooth crossover singers to 1990s blockbuster albums and younger artists moving between country and pop markets. Glen Campbell's By the Time I Get to Phoenix, Crystal Gayle's Don't It Make My Brown Eyes Blue, Dolly Parton's Here You Come Again, and Kenny Rogers' Lucille give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
scene_description.deep: Country-pop has appeared in waves, from smooth crossover singers to 1990s blockbuster albums and younger artists moving between country and pop markets. The hook is polished and immediate, while twang, narrative, or country imagery remains legible. Glen Campbell's By the Time I Get to Phoenix, Crystal Gayle's Don't It Make My Brown Eyes Blue, Dolly Parton's Here You Come Again, and Kenny Rogers' Lucille give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

Etta James' I'd Rather Go Blind, Green Onions - Booker T. & the M.G.'s, Wilson Pickett's In the Midnight Hour, and Sam & Dave's Hold On, I'm Comin' give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
scene_description.deep: Southern soul took shape through Memphis and Muscle Shoals studios where church-trained voices met hard-working rhythm sections and horn arrangements. The records feel live, sweaty, and vocally urgent even when the writing is tightly crafted. Etta James' I'd Rather Go Blind, Green Onions - Booker T. & the M.G.'s, Wilson Pickett's In the Midnight Hour, and Sam & Dave's Hold On, I'm Comin' give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

scene_description.compact: Old-school hip-hop grew from Bronx block parties and DJ practices into records that introduced rap to national and global audiences.
scene_description.standard: Old-school hip-hop grew from Bronx block parties and DJ practices into records that introduced rap to national and global audiences. The Sugarhill Gang's Rapper's Delight, Kurtis Blow's The Breaks, Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five's The Message, and Run-DMC's It's Like That give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
scene_description.deep: Old-school hip-hop grew from Bronx block parties and DJ practices into records that introduced rap to national and global audiences. The energy is direct, rhythmic, and functional: move the party, display skill, and make the beat speak. The Sugarhill Gang's Rapper's Delight, Kurtis Blow's The Breaks, Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five's The Message, and Run-DMC's It's Like That give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

atlas_home_region_card.compact: A downtown New York scene/ecosystem where punk urgency, art-school experiment, poetry, pop instincts, minimal electronics, and club culture collided around CBGB and nearby venues rather than resolving into one sound.
atlas_home_region_card.standard: This scene changed what a rock band could be after the 1960s. It helped punk and new wave separate from classic-rock scale, proved that small rooms and original songs could generate durable lineages, and opened roads into post-punk, college rock, indie, noise rock, synth-punk, art-pop, and modern downtown/retro-shadow guitar music. mission_detail_history_module.compact: What this route tests: A downtown New York scene/ecosystem where punk urgency, art-school experiment, poetry, pop instincts, minimal electronics, and club culture collided around CBGB and nearby venues rather than resolving into one sound.
mission_detail_history_module.standard: CBGB opened in 1973 on the Bowery under Hilly Kristal and became a practical home for original underground rock. What later looks like “the CBGB sound” was actually a cluster of incompatible but mutually intensifying bands: Patti Smith fused rock and poetry; Television stretched guitar interplay into nervous art-rock; Talking Heads turned anxiety, rhythm, and conceptual framing into new wave; Blondie smuggled girl-group/pop/disco instincts through downtown cool; Richard Hell gave punk a persona of damaged refusal; Suicide reduced rock to voice, synth pulse, and menace; and No Wave pushed the scene toward abrasive boundary testing. It helps place this road in a broader music-history context.
mission_detail_history_module.deep: CBGB opened in 1973 on the Bowery under Hilly Kristal and became a practical home for original underground rock. What later looks like “the CBGB sound” was actually a cluster of incompatible but mutually intensifying bands: Patti Smith fused rock and poetry; Television stretched guitar interplay into nervous art-rock; Talking Heads turned anxiety, rhythm, and conceptual framing into new wave; Blondie smuggled girl-group/pop/disco instincts through downtown cool; Richard Hell gave punk a persona of damaged refusal; Suicide reduced rock to voice, synth pulse, and menace; and No Wave pushed the scene toward abrasive boundary testing. This scene changed what a rock band could be after the 1960s. It helped punk and new wave separate from classic-rock scale, proved that small rooms and original songs could generate durable lineages, and opened roads into post-punk, college rock, indie, noise rock, synth-punk, art-pop, and modern downtown/retro-shadow guitar music. Historically important does not automatically mean user-specific fit: Atlas should treat each branch as a separate test.

did_you_know_card.compact: The initials came from “Country, Bluegrass, Blues,” but the club became famous because it gave original underground rock bands a room, a stage, and a scene.
did_you_know_card.standard: CBGB mattered because it gave incompatible original bands the same room. Patti Smith, Television, Blondie, Suicide, and James Chance prove this was a scene, not one sound.

scene_description.compact: Doom inherits Sabbath's dark weight; stoner and desert heavy add fuzz, groove, repetition, and psychedelic space.
scene_description.standard: Doom inherits Sabbath's dark weight; stoner and desert heavy add fuzz, groove, repetition, and psychedelic space. Black Sabbath's Into the Void, Monster Magnet's Space Lord, Kyuss' Welcome to Sky Valley, and Queens of the Stone Age's Rated R give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
scene_description.deep: Doom inherits Sabbath's dark weight; stoner and desert heavy add fuzz, groove, repetition, and psychedelic space. Instead of speed or flash, the distinct feature is mass: tone, repetition, and atmosphere carry the drama. Black Sabbath's Into the Void, Monster Magnet's Space Lord, Kyuss' Welcome to Sky Valley, and Queens of the Stone Age's Rated R give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

scene_description.compact: This road is for gateway versions of extreme metal, where the listener can hear how metal splits into brutality, atmosphere, corrosion, and complexity.

From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

Interpol's PDA, Bloc Party's Like Eating Glass, Yeah Yeah Yeahs' Date with the Night, and Franz Ferdinand's Take Me Out give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
region_scene_page.deep: This road follows bands that made older post-punk moves feel new inside the blog/indie era: sharp guitars, cool surfaces, and rhythm you can dance to. The distinction is angularity and mood: darker, more bass-driven, and more mannered than simple garage rock revival. Interpol's PDA, Bloc Party's Like Eating Glass, Yeah Yeah Yeahs' Date with the Night, and Franz Ferdinand's Take Me Out give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

scene_description.compact: House emerged from Chicago dance spaces where DJs, drum machines, disco memory, queer nightlife, and Black and Latino club culture made a new electronic pulse.
scene_description.standard: House emerged from Chicago dance spaces where DJs, drum machines, disco memory, queer nightlife, and Black and Latino club culture made a new electronic pulse. Steve "Silk" Hurley's Jack Your Body, Farley Jackmaster Funk featuring Darryl Pandy's Love Can't Turn Around, Frankie Knuckles, and Inner City's Good Life give the scene its high-recognition landmarks.
scene_description.deep: House emerged from Chicago dance spaces where DJs, drum machines, disco memory, queer nightlife, and Black and Latino club culture made a new electronic pulse. Unlike techno's colder futurism, house keeps a warmer relationship to disco, soul, vocals, and communal release. Steve "Silk" Hurley's Jack Your Body, Farley Jackmaster Funk featuring Darryl Pandy's Love Can't Turn Around, Frankie Knuckles, and Inner City's Good Life give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.

Kesha's Tik Tok, Justin Timberlake's Cry Me a River, Beyoncé's Crazy in Love, and The Pussycat Dolls featuring Snoop Dogg's Buttons give the scene its high-recognition landmarks. From there, the examples move from quick recognition toward medium and deeper scene signals.
